playoff final to reach the second tier of English football for the first time in the history of the

it proved to be merely a minor setback for the Matthew Benham Revolution. The following season,

stadium and one promotion to the Premier League, this time winning at Wembley in the championship

Premier League. The Glovers had the lowest budget in League One when they won promotion to the

Yovell were the division's favourites to be relegated and the longest odds to win promotion.
Sadly for Yovell, who had spent more than 90% of their existence as a non-league team,
that playoff final win, which was the greatest day in the history of the club,
also proved to be the beginning of the end in terms of their extraordinary success.
Within just two and a half years of winning on the hallow turf of Wembley Stadium,
Yovell found themselves glued to the foot of the league two table, following consecutive 24
place finishes in the championship and in League One and in 2019, Yovell finally lost their football
ball league status. To look at the rise and fall of Yovell Town in the abstract,
you might say that Yovell is a small, fairly remote town of just 45,000 people
and that not only have Yovell Town spent almost the entirety of their existence playing non-league
football, they are the only club from Somerset ever to have played enough football league.
It is tempting their fourth to say a Yovell Town's rise from 2003 to 2013 really,
that it was a freak event and that they're demise in the near decades since,

around Saturn's North Pole that science cannot yet explain. They don't just rise fall,
implode or explode without reasonable explanation, which means that it is worth asking the question
of just how Yovell Town managed to pull off one of the most dramatic rises and catastrophic
collapses in the history of English football, all in the space of barely more than a decade.
So sit back, relax and join me on a journey to Somerset, as we take a look at how Yovell Town went
from the archetypal non-league team to the football league's greatest overachievers and then back
again in about the same amount of time as it would take you to get from Yovell to anywhere with
the population of more than 100,000 people. Although Yovell didn't become a football league team
for the first time until 2003, for more than a century before that, they were no strangers to
playing and indeed beating League opposition. In fact, Yovell still hold the record for having
one more games, 21 to be precise, against League opposition as a non-league team than any other club.
Yovell dumped the likes of Fulham and Blackpool out of the FA Cup in famous cup upsets,
but their most notable giant killing came in 1949, when First Division Sunderland,
then the richest club in Britain, got beat to one at Hewish Athletic Ground,
sending Yovell into a fifth round tie against Manchester United. That match would prove to be a
step too far for Yovell, who lost eight-nil at Main Road in front of a crowd of more than 81,000 people,
as Old Trafford was still undergoing reconstruction as a result of World War II bombing.
Throughout this time, of giant killings and Southern League titles, Yovell had often applied
to join the Football League. Prior to 1986, there was no promotional
relegation between what we now call League 2 and the National League, but rather,
teams would be infrequently elected to join the Football League based upon the votes of existing
members. Yovell came within a whisker of being admitted in 1976, but the year before promotion
and relegation between the League and non-league games was actually introduced,
Yovell were relegated down into the Ismian League, which was the sixth tier of English football at the
time. It was a real blow to Yovell, but they bounced back in 1988 and in 1990, they moved into their
new home ground, Hewish Park. Whilst the club's old stadium, the Hewish Athletic Ground, better
known simply as Hewish, certainly had its charms, the eight-foot slope from one sideline to the other,
for which it was famous, had previously proved to be a real hurdle to Yovell being granted admission
to the Football League. With that ultimate aim in mind, Yovell moved into the new Hewish Park,

and it was at the start of the new millennium that something special started to take place in

Johnson was able to instill a winning mentality in his players from that moment on,

but they very quickly made it clear that they weren't just there to make up their numbers.
In their first season playing in the third division, soon to be renamed League 2,
Yovell finished above established football league sides like Swansea City and
relatively nearby Bristol Rovers, and they only missed out on the playoffs to Lincoln City
by virtue of goal difference. That was a bitter pill to swallow at the end of what had been
a sensational debut campaign in the football league, but there would be nothing bitter
about the season that followed. Over the summer, despite selling Gavin Williams to West Ham for
roughly a quarter of a million pounds and not spending a single penny on new arrivals,
Yovell brought in some outstanding players as free agents.
The most notable of them was undoubtedly Phil Jevons, who had only scored three goals
on Loner Hall City the previous season, but had previously doubled figures in the third tier
whilst playing for Grimsby Town. He struck a whopping 27 times in the league and 29 times in

Exhilarating to watch, Yovell actually conceded more goals that season than last
placed Cambridge United despite winning the title by virtue of the fact that they scored 90 goals.
This was Champagne football, at least by the standards of league 2, and a record average of
6320 fans flocked to see the glove as make history in such emphatic style, the fourth

The remarkable work that Gary Johnson had done at Yovell Town had not gone unnoticed though,
and when the Bristol City Board lost patience with manager Brian Tinian at the beginning

There would be more disruption midway through Yovell's first season playing in league 1,

Webb, a former professional footballer himself, best known for the six years that he spent,
as a regular starter at Chelsea, had actually briefly managed Yovell in the year 2000,
and he appointed himself as the club's new chief executive. His time in the job would be
very short-lived, lasting just two months, but despite all of the turmoil off the pitch,
Yovell gave a solid account of themselves in league 1 under Gary Johnson's former assistant,
Steve Thompson, who was entrusted with the top job in his absence, finishing 15th in league 1.
Thompson was still replaced over the summer by Russell Slade, who had just lost a playoff
final at Grimsby Town, and the 2006-07 season would be the most emphatic illustration yet
of how far Yovell Town had come. Just three points separated Yovell,
and two-time European champions Nottingham Forest at the end of the season,
which meant that the two teams met in the playoff semi-finals,

It was also the second season in a row, which heralded a change of ownership at Yovell Town,

The following season, whilst Yovell felt when 18th place finished in league 1,

Over the summer, the Glovers did some fantastic work in the loan market,

the feeling of winning at Wembley. After beating another,
comparative giants in the form of Sheffield United in the semi-finals,
before holding firm to prevent a brilliant footballing side in Brentford in the final.
The championship was the promised land as far as Yovell's town were concerned.
From the Ismian League, English football sixth tier, as recently as 1997,
Yovell were now just one division below the Premier League and would be playing teams like
Darby County, Leeds United and Sheffield Wednesday, who previously they would have targeted as giant

the greatest achievement in the history of Yovell's town football club,
would be the beginning of the end for English football's greatest underdogs.
Or, at least, that was the case in the eyes of then Chairman John Fry. As far as Fry is concerned,
it was the investment required following promotion, and the shortfall that the club then had when
they were relegated from the championship that led to their rapid demise. That might seem like
a curious assessment to some people, perhaps even to some Yovell town fans, given that the club,

and Championship revenues. No such system exists for when a team is relegated from the championship,
but for Yovell town, given the size of the club and their attendances, that gap felt almost as large.
One of the club's most significant costs following promotion was the creation of an academy system.
When they won promotion from League 1, the lovers didn't even have a youth or a reserve team,

despite Yovell being so widely tipped to be relegated that season that,

Rooted to the foot of the league one table, from February until the end of the season,

Yovell survived that season, but only just, marking the first of three seasons,

In December 2015, another club legend, Darren Waye, replaced Paul Staric as first-team boss.

to have been kept Yovell in the football league, but immediately after he signed that deal,

The National League is an incredibly competitive division, with just one automatic promotion place,
